VIDEO.title: The Hidden Message Behind New Wine & Old Wineskins REVEALED! (Matthew 9:1-17)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: Know the God of the Scriptures.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 9:1-17. Back in His own city, Capernaum, Jesus forgives and heals a paralytic, calls Matthew the tax collector, eats with tax collectors and sinners, and answers John's disciples about fasting with sayings about a bridegroom, patches and wineskins. Luke 5:17-39 adds details.

Recap: in chapter 4 Jesus begins His ministry; in chapters 5-7 He preaches the sermon, rightly interpreting (fulfilling) the Torah from the heart; in chapters 8-9 He walks out His teaching for His disciples to see.

Many in the first century linked sickness with sin (John 5:14; 1 Corinthians 11:30). Jesus uses that to teach that He has authority to forgive sins, which only Yahweh can do (Exodus 34:7; Psalm 32:5). 'Son of Man' points to Daniel 7:13-14. The crowd is afraid; the scribes cry 'blasphemy.'

Matthew is not a promising young Pharisee but the epitome of the outcast: a tax collector, seen as a liar and a collaborator. Criticized for eating with sinners, Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 in its Greek form, 'mercy and not sacrifice,' pointing back to 'Blessed are the merciful' (5:7), the center of the Beatitudes.

The new garment and new wine echo Isaiah: garments of salvation and a bridegroom (Isaiah 61:10), Israel as God's vineyard (Isaiah 5:7; 27:2-6), and mountains dripping with sweet wine (Joel 3:18). The video's reading: Jesus' teaching is new wine, His chosen disciples are the fresh wineskins, and the Pharisees, who prefer the old (Luke 5:39), are old wineskins.

The lesson: it is possible to know the Scriptures of God without knowing the God of the Scriptures. The Pharisees knew Tanakh but not God's merciful heart, His good eye (6:22), toward outcasts. Is that possible today?
QUOTES: It is possible to know the scriptures of God while not knowing the God of the scriptures.
Jesus is not replacing God's law. He is reteaching it from the perspective of the heart.
He also wants them to be experts at loving God, which requires your heart as well.

method.p: The teacher's tip: if you have a physical Bible, lay Luke 5:17-39 open next to Matthew 9:1-17 and note the extra details Luke gives: the roof, the Pharisees from Jerusalem, Levi's big reception, and 'The old is good enough.'

LSB_QUOTES.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—then He said to the paralytic, “Get up, pick up your bed and go home.”
But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire compassion, and not sacrifice,’ for I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.
but they put new wine into fresh wineskins, and both are preserved.

src.text: And behold, they brought to Him a paralytic lying on a bed. Seeing their faith, Jesus said to the paralytic, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.” And behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man blasphemes.”

lines.text: In the first century, sickness was widely linked to sin (John 5:14; 1 Corinthians 11:30). Jesus uses that view to teach that He has power to forgive sins (9:2, 6).
Mark and Luke tell how the friends dug through the roof to lower him (Mark 2:4; Luke 5:19). 'Seeing their faith': the friends' faith, too.

src.text: Yahweh, Yahweh God, compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in lovingkindness and truth; who keeps lovingkindness for thousands, who forgives iniquity, transgression, and sin;

right.text: I, even I, am the one who wipes out your transgressions for My own sake, / And I will not remember your sins.

lines.text: Only Yahweh can forgive sins. Psalm 32:5, Jeremiah 33 and Isaiah 43 say the same.
Mark and Luke spell out the scribes' objection: 'who can forgive sins but God alone?' (Mark 2:7).

left.text: And behold, with the clouds of heaven / One like a Son of Man was coming, / ... And to Him was given dominion, / Glory, and a kingdom,

right.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins

lines.text: By saying these things aloud, Jesus signals to those who know their Scripture to go back and explore what He is claiming. The Son of Man has authority in His own kingdom.

src.text: But when the crowds saw this, they were afraid, and glorified God, who had given such authority to men.

lines.text: The crowd is afraid, awestruck, rather than excited; the scribes whisper 'blasphemy.' The same act divides people.
Chrysostom notes that at first Jesus did not say 'I forgive,' but 'your sins be forgiven you': 'upon their constraining, He discloses His authority more clearly' (Homilies on Matthew 29).

src.text: And as Jesus went on from there, He saw a man called Matthew, sitting in the tax office; and He said to him, “Follow Me!” And he stood up and followed Him.

lines.text: Tax collectors were private contractors who charged tolls on goods carried along certain roads, like a toll booth. Many overcharged and pocketed the profit, so they were seen as liars and collaborators. Calling one to be a disciple would have shocked anyone.

Rabbinic law groups tax collectors with murderers and robbers (Mishnah Nedarim 3:4), forbids taking change from their chests (Mishnah Bava Kamma 10:1), and disqualifies those who overcharge as witnesses (Talmud, Sanhedrin 25b). Mark and Luke call him Levi (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27).
Chrysostom: 'from the midst of the evils He drew him up' (Homilies on Matthew 30).

left.text: For I delight in lovingkindness rather than sacrifice, / And in the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.

right.text: But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire compassion, and not sacrifice,’ for I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.

lines.text: Hosea's Hebrew word is chesed, steadfast love. Jesus quotes the Greek version (the Septuagint), which reads eleos, mercy, to point back to 'Blessed are the merciful' (5:7), the center of the Beatitudes.
The rest of Hosea's verse matters too: God wants 'the knowledge of God,' not just knowledge of His law. That takes the heart as well as the mind.
Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 again in 12:7: 'you would not have condemned the innocent.'

left.text: He executes justice for the orphan and the widow, and shows love for the sojourner by giving him food and clothing. So show love for the sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.

right.text: Yahweh builds up Jerusalem; / He gathers the outcasts of Israel.

lines.text: God is for the outcast, and His kingdom spreads through those who become like their Father. The Pharisees knew Tanakh and should have known this.
Greater righteousness (5:20) is not more actions but righteousness that pierces and transforms the heart. Jesus spends time with the people the Pharisees have no time for.

WINE.title: While the bridegroom is with them

src.text: Then the disciples of John came to Him, asking, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but Your disciples do not fast?” And Jesus said to them, “Can the attendants of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast.”

lines.text: Not all of John's disciples shared Jesus' outlook. If Jesus' disciples did not fast, Jesus did not either.
Weddings were week-long celebrations; guests were excused from fasting. 'Taken away' hints at the cross. John himself called Jesus the bridegroom (John 3:29).

left.text: But no one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment; for the patch pulls away from the garment, and a worse tear results.

right.text: For He has clothed me with garments of salvation, / He has wrapped me with a robe of righteousness, / As a bridegroom decks himself with a headdress, / And as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.

lines.text: A patch implies you need a whole new garment. Jesus read Isaiah 61 in Nazareth and said, 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing' (Luke 4:21). Read on: an everlasting covenant (61:8), God's people called priests (61:6), new clothes, and a bridegroom and bride.
'Decks himself' is the Hebrew kahan (H3547), to act as a priest: the bridegroom dresses like a priest.

left.text: For the vineyard of Yahweh of hosts is the house of Israel / And the men of Judah His delightful plant.

right.text: And it will be in that day, / That the mountains will drip with sweet wine,

lines.text: Israel was understood as God's vineyard. In Isaiah 27 God promises to redeem it so that it will 'fill the whole world with produce' (Isaiah 27:6). Joel pictures the last days dripping with sweet wine.
Jesus later says, 'I am the vine, you are the branches' (John 15:5).

src.text: Nor do people put new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, and the wine pours out and the wineskins are ruined; but they put new wine into fresh wineskins, and both are preserved.

right.text: And no one, after drinking old wine wishes for new; for he says, ‘The old is good enough.’

lines.text: The video's reading: Jesus' new wine (His teaching, His proclamation of the kingdom, His right interpretation of Torah) must go into fresh wineskins, the disciples He has chosen, not old wineskins like the Pharisees, who prefer their old understanding. The teacher adds, 'I could be wrong about that.'
Chrysostom saw the same Old Testament flavor: 'Do you see His illustrations, how like the Old Testament? The garment? The wine skins?' (Homilies on Matthew 30).

TERMS.def: Speaking against God or claiming what is His alone, such as the right to forgive sins.
Jesus' title for Himself, from Daniel 7:13-14: one given dominion and a kingdom.
A contractor who collected tolls or taxes for the ruling power; many overcharged and kept the profit.
Notorious law-breakers, or those outside the Pharisees' standards of purity.
The Greek translation of the Old Testament. Matthew 9:13 follows its 'mercy' (eleos) in Hosea 6:6.
Hebrew for steadfast love or lovingkindness (Hosea 6:6).
Hebrew 'good eye': a generous, merciful view of others (6:22).
Goatskin bags for wine. New wine still ferments and stretches the skin; an old, stiff skin bursts.
Going without food in mourning or prayer; Pharisees fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12).

WORDS.gloss: Mercy, compassion. Look up: BDAG, ἔλεος.
To act as a priest; 'decks himself' in Isa 61:10.

BACKGROUND.p: Houses were built of basalt with flat roofs of beams, branches and packed earth, reached by an outside stair. Digging through one was possible, and repairable.
Capernaum sat near the border between Herod Antipas' Galilee and Philip's territory, on a trade route. Goods crossing the border paid tolls, collected by contractors like Matthew.
Sharing a meal meant accepting someone. Pharisees guarded purity at the table, so eating with sinners looked like approving of them.
New cloth shrinks when washed and tears an old garment. New wine keeps fermenting; it needs a fresh skin that can stretch.

DEBATES.p: Some passages link them (John 5:14; 1 Corinthians 11:30), but Jesus rejects a simple rule: 'Neither this man nor his parents sinned' (John 9:3). In 9:2 He addresses the man's deeper need first.

DEBATES.h: What are the new wine and the wineskins?
DEBATES.p: The video: Jesus' teaching, and His chosen disciples. Others: the kingdom's new age that old forms (like fasting rules) cannot hold, or the new covenant itself. The teacher says he could be wrong.
Jesus says His disciples will fast 'when the bridegroom is taken away' (9:15), and in 6:16-18 assumes they will. The early church fasted (Acts 13:2-3; Didache 8).
Mark and Luke call him Levi; Matthew's Gospel calls him Matthew. Most think he had two names, like Simon Peter.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: Caption references: 'Hosea 66' is Hosea 6:6; 'Isaiah 6:18' is Isaiah 61:8; 'Deuteronomy 10:1 19' is 10:18-19; and the sermon is Matthew 5-7 (the captions say 5:7).
Isaiah 27:2 reads 'A vineyard of delight' in the LSB. The video's 'vineyard of wine' follows a variant Hebrew reading found in some manuscripts and translations.
Capernaum was in Herod Antipas' territory, so Matthew most likely collected tolls for Antipas rather than directly for Rome. People still saw such collectors as serving the foreign-backed rulers.

The rabbinic rules come from the Mishnah (c. AD 200) and the Talmud (c. AD 500): tax collectors are grouped with murderers and robbers (Nedarim 3:4), no change from their chest (Bava Kamma 10:1), and overchargers barred as witnesses (Sanhedrin 25b). Being put out of the synagogue was not found in these sources.

QUESTIONS: The friends' faith brought the paralytic to Jesus. Who could you carry to Him?
Why would 'your sins are forgiven' be harder to say than 'get up and walk'?
Who are the 'tax collectors and sinners' your church might avoid? What would eating with them look like?
'Go and learn what this means.' How do you move from knowing Scripture to knowing God?
Are you more like the old wineskin ('The old is good enough') or the new? Where are you resisting something Jesus wants to do?
Is it possible to know the Scriptures of God without knowing the God of the Scriptures today? Gut check: what about you?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson for the original audience: it is possible to know the Scriptures of God while not knowing the God of the Scriptures. By asking why Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners, the Pharisees proved they lacked the knowledge God desired. God wants His people to be experts not only in His law, which needs the mind, but in loving Him, which needs the heart. Then they would have His merciful heart and see the world through His good eye, and see what Jesus saw in these outcasts. The lesson echoes through time: is it possible today? Think about how this applies directly to your life so that you can do something about it.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): Jesus said, 'go and learn what this means' (9:13). This week read Hosea 6:1-6 slowly, then share a meal or a coffee with someone on the margins of your circle. Afterward, ask what you learned about God's heart, not just about the text.

   (video) Only Yahweh can forgive sins. Psalm 32:5, Jeremiah 33 and Isaiah 43 say the same. (Psalm 32:5; Jeremiah 33:8)
   [Background] Mark and Luke spell out the scribes' objection: 'who can forgive sins but God alone?' (Mark 2:7). (Mark 2:7)
3. Son of Man · Daniel 7:13-14: Authority on earth
   Daniel's vision (Daniel 7:13-14, LSB): "And behold, with the clouds of heaven / One like a Son of Man was coming, / ... And to Him was given dominion, / Glory, and a kingdom,"
   Jesus (Matthew 9:6, LSB): "But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins"
   (video) By saying these things aloud, Jesus signals to those who know their Scripture to go back and explore what He is claiming. The Son of Man has authority in His own kingdom.
4. The crowd splits · Matthew 9:8: Afraid, and glorifying God
   Reactions Matthew 9:8: "But when the crowds saw this, they were afraid, and glorified God, who had given such authority to men." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+9:8
   (video) The crowd is afraid, awestruck, rather than excited; the scribes whisper 'blasphemy.' The same act divides people.
   [Background] Chrysostom notes that at first Jesus did not say 'I forgive,' but 'your sins be forgiven you': 'upon their constraining, He discloses His authority more clearly' (Homilies on Matthew 29).

## Mercy and not sacrifice
1. Matthew's call · Matthew 9:9: Follow Me!
   Outcast Matthew 9:9: "And as Jesus went on from there, He saw a man called Matthew, sitting in the tax office; and He said to him, “Follow Me!” And he stood up and followed Him." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+9:9
   (video) Tax collectors were private contractors who charged tolls on goods carried along certain roads, like a toll booth. Many overcharged and pocketed the profit, so they were seen as liars and collaborators. Calling one to be a disciple would have shocked anyone.
   [Background] Rabbinic law groups tax collectors with murderers and robbers (Mishnah Nedarim 3:4), forbids taking change from their chests (Mishnah Bava Kamma 10:1), and disqualifies those who overcharge as witnesses (Talmud, Sanhedrin 25b). Mark and Luke call him Levi (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27). (Mark 2:14)
   [Background] Chrysostom: 'from the midst of the evils He drew him up' (Homilies on Matthew 30).
2. The physician · Matthew 9:10-13: I desire compassion
   Hosea (Hosea 6:6, LSB): "For I delight in lovingkindness rather than sacrifice, / And in the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings."
   Jesus (Matthew 9:13, LSB): "But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire compassion, and not sacrifice,’ for I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners."
   (video) Hosea's Hebrew word is chesed, steadfast love. Jesus quotes the Greek version (the Septuagint), which reads eleos, mercy, to point back to 'Blessed are the merciful' (5:7), the center of the Beatitudes. (Matthew 5:7)
   (video) The rest of Hosea's verse matters too: God wants 'the knowledge of God,' not just knowledge of His law. That takes the heart as well as the mind.
   [Background] Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 again in 12:7: 'you would not have condemned the innocent.' (Matthew 12:7)
3. God for the outcast: He gathers the outcasts
   Moses (Deuteronomy 10:18-19, LSB): "He executes justice for the orphan and the widow, and shows love for the sojourner by giving him food and clothing. So show love for the sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt."
   Psalms (Psalm 147:2, LSB): "Yahweh builds up Jerusalem; / He gathers the outcasts of Israel."
   (video) God is for the outcast, and His kingdom spreads through those who become like their Father. The Pharisees knew Tanakh and should have known this. (Isaiah 56:7-8)
   (video) Greater righteousness (5:20) is not more actions but righteousness that pierces and transforms the heart. Jesus spends time with the people the Pharisees have no time for. (Matthew 5:20)

## Bridegroom, garments and wine
1. The bridegroom · Matthew 9:14-15: While the bridegroom is with them
   Feast Matthew 9:14-15: "Then the disciples of John came to Him, asking, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but Your disciples do not fast?” And Jesus said to them, “Can the attendants of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+9:14-15
   (video) Not all of John's disciples shared Jesus' outlook. If Jesus' disciples did not fast, Jesus did not either.
   [Background] Weddings were week-long celebrations; guests were excused from fasting. 'Taken away' hints at the cross. John himself called Jesus the bridegroom (John 3:29). (John 3:29)
2. The new garment · Isaiah 61: Garments of salvation
   Jesus (Matthew 9:16, LSB): "But no one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment; for the patch pulls away from the garment, and a worse tear results."
   Isaiah (Isaiah 61:10, LSB): "For He has clothed me with garments of salvation, / He has wrapped me with a robe of righteousness, / As a bridegroom decks himself with a headdress, / And as a bride adorns herself with her jewels."
   (video) A patch implies you need a whole new garment. Jesus read Isaiah 61 in Nazareth and said, 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing' (Luke 4:21). Read on: an everlasting covenant (61:8), God's people called priests (61:6), new clothes, and a bridegroom and bride. (Luke 4:21; Isaiah 61:6; Isaiah 61:8)
   [Background] 'Decks himself' is the Hebrew kahan (H3547), to act as a priest: the bridegroom dresses like a priest.
3. The vineyard · Isaiah 5 and 27: Israel, God's vineyard
   Isaiah 5 (Isaiah 5:7, LSB): "For the vineyard of Yahweh of hosts is the house of Israel / And the men of Judah His delightful plant."
   Joel (Joel 3:18, LSB): "And it will be in that day, / That the mountains will drip with sweet wine,"
   (video) Israel was understood as God's vineyard. In Isaiah 27 God promises to redeem it so that it will 'fill the whole world with produce' (Isaiah 27:6). Joel pictures the last days dripping with sweet wine. (Isaiah 27:2-6)
   [Background] Jesus later says, 'I am the vine, you are the branches' (John 15:5). (John 15:5)
4. The wineskins · Matthew 9:17: New wine, fresh wineskins
   Luke (Luke 5:39, LSB): "And no one, after drinking old wine wishes for new; for he says, ‘The old is good enough.’"
   New Matthew 9:17: "Nor do people put new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, and the wine pours out and the wineskins are ruined; but they put new wine into fresh wineskins, and both are preserved." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+9:17
   (video) The video's reading: Jesus' new wine (His teaching, His proclamation of the kingdom, His right interpretation of Torah) must go into fresh wineskins, the disciples He has chosen, not old wineskins like the Pharisees, who prefer their old understanding. The teacher adds, 'I could be wrong about that.'
   [Background] Chrysostom saw the same Old Testament flavor: 'Do you see His illustrations, how like the Old Testament? The garment? The wine skins?' (Homilies on Matthew 30).

## Key people
- Jesus: Forgives sins with divine authority, calls an outcast, eats with sinners, and keeps walking out His sermon. [Background] 'His own city' (9:1) is Capernaum (4:13).
- The paralytic and his friends: Healed so Jesus can teach about His authority to forgive. [Background] Mark: four men carried him and dug through the roof (Mark 2:3-4).
- The scribes: Say to themselves, 'This man blasphemes.' [Background] Blasphemy here means claiming what belongs to God alone.
- Matthew (Levi): A tax collector, the epitome of the outcast, called to be a disciple. [Background] Listed as 'Matthew the tax collector' among the Twelve (10:3); tradition names him the Gospel's author.
- Tax collectors and sinners: Social outcasts who show the mercy-hungry heart God is looking for. [Background] 'Sinners' meant notorious law-breakers, or those who did not keep the Pharisees' standards.
- The Pharisees: Experts in Tanakh who still do not understand why God would spend time with outcasts. [Background] Pharisees ate with strict purity rules; table fellowship marked who belonged.
- John's disciples: Fast like the Pharisees and ask why Jesus' disciples do not. [Background] John was in prison by now (4:12).

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum (named in the video): 'His own city' (9:1): the paralytic, and Matthew's tax office.
- Kursi: The east shore Jesus left behind (8:28-9:1).
- Bethsaida: Across the Jordan in Philip's territory: Capernaum was the first town in Antipas' land, a natural place for tolls.
- Magdala: A fishing and trade town on the road south.
- Tiberias: Herod Antipas' capital, who controlled Galilee's taxes.

## Key terms
- Blasphemy: Speaking against God or claiming what is His alone, such as the right to forgive sins.
- Son of Man: Jesus' title for Himself, from Daniel 7:13-14: one given dominion and a kingdom.
- Tax collector: A contractor who collected tolls or taxes for the ruling power; many overcharged and kept the profit.
- Sinners: Notorious law-breakers, or those outside the Pharisees' standards of purity. [Background]
- Septuagint: The Greek translation of the Old Testament. Matthew 9:13 follows its 'mercy' (eleos) in Hosea 6:6.
- Chesed: Hebrew for steadfast love or lovingkindness (Hosea 6:6).
- Ayin tovah: Hebrew 'good eye': a generous, merciful view of others (6:22).
- Wineskins: Goatskin bags for wine. New wine still ferments and stretches the skin; an old, stiff skin bursts. [Background]
- Fasting: Going without food in mourning or prayer; Pharisees fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12). [Background]

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Roofs in Capernaum: Houses were built of basalt with flat roofs of beams, branches and packed earth, reached by an outside stair. Digging through one was possible, and repairable.
- Tolls on the road: Capernaum sat near the border between Herod Antipas' Galilee and Philip's territory, on a trade route. Goods crossing the border paid tolls, collected by contractors like Matthew.
- Table fellowship: Sharing a meal meant accepting someone. Pharisees guarded purity at the table, so eating with sinners looked like approving of them.
- Wineskins and unshrunk cloth: New cloth shrinks when washed and tears an old garment. New wine keeps fermenting; it needs a fresh skin that can stretch.

- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "For such is the quality of a physician; unless he endure the corruption of the sick, he frees them not from their infirmity." Homilies on Matthew 30, on 9:12. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Is sickness caused by sin? Some passages link them (John 5:14; 1 Corinthians 11:30), but Jesus rejects a simple rule: 'Neither this man nor his parents sinned' (John 9:3). In 9:2 He addresses the man's deeper need first.
- What are the new wine and the wineskins? The video: Jesus' teaching, and His chosen disciples. Others: the kingdom's new age that old forms (like fasting rules) cannot hold, or the new covenant itself. The teacher says he could be wrong.
- Should Christians fast? Jesus says His disciples will fast 'when the bridegroom is taken away' (9:15), and in 6:16-18 assumes they will. The early church fasted (Acts 13:2-3; Didache 8).
- Matthew and Levi Mark and Luke call him Levi; Matthew's Gospel calls him Matthew. Most think he had two names, like Simon Peter.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- Caption references: 'Hosea 66' is Hosea 6:6; 'Isaiah 6:18' is Isaiah 61:8; 'Deuteronomy 10:1 19' is 10:18-19; and the sermon is Matthew 5-7 (the captions say 5:7).
- Isaiah 27:2 reads 'A vineyard of delight' in the LSB. The video's 'vineyard of wine' follows a variant Hebrew reading found in some manuscripts and translations.
- Capernaum was in Herod Antipas' territory, so Matthew most likely collected tolls for Antipas rather than directly for Rome. People still saw such collectors as serving the foreign-backed rulers.
- The rabbinic rules come from the Mishnah (c. AD 200) and the Talmud (c. AD 500): tax collectors are grouped with murderers and robbers (Nedarim 3:4), no change from their chest (Bava Kamma 10:1), and overchargers barred as witnesses (Sanhedrin 25b). Being put out of the synagogue was not found in these sources.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. The friends' faith brought the paralytic to Jesus. Who could you carry to Him?
2. Why would 'your sins are forgiven' be harder to say than 'get up and walk'?
3. Who are the 'tax collectors and sinners' your church might avoid? What would eating with them look like?
4. 'Go and learn what this means.' How do you move from knowing Scripture to knowing God?
5. Are you more like the old wineskin ('The old is good enough') or the new? Where are you resisting something Jesus wants to do?
6. Is it possible to know the Scriptures of God without knowing the God of the Scriptures today? Gut check: what about you?

## Application
- (video) The lesson for the original audience: it is possible to know the Scriptures of God while not knowing the God of the Scriptures. By asking why Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners, the Pharisees proved they lacked the knowledge God desired. God wants His people to be experts not only in His law, which needs the mind, but in loving Him, which needs the heart. Then they would have His merciful heart and see the world through His good eye, and see what Jesus saw in these outcasts. The lesson echoes through time: is it possible today? Think about how this applies directly to your life so that you can do something about it.
- Study note (added): Jesus said, 'go and learn what this means' (9:13). This week read Hosea 6:1-6 slowly, then share a meal or a coffee with someone on the margins of your circle. Afterward, ask what you learned about God's heart, not just about the text.
